posts.name: S.Vignesh
posts.cooked:
I want to know how the assignments are set up in the VM. Especially the synchro commands. I want to be able to do that on my local WSL.

I have already downloaded the se2001 directory in home directory and the /opt directory from the VM to my WSL.

I even tried copying the synchro binary file to my local usr/local/bin.

If anybody has some idea on how all this works and is able to provide some guidance, it will be much appreciated.

I just like the idea of having all the assignments on a local system to practice whenever needed instead of relying on the VM, even past the completion of the course.

On a side note when I was looking around the internet for some answers I did come across the rsync command which seems to be useful in maintaining an incremental backup.

But this seems to work only from one linux machine to another. My client machine is windows so I don’t know how to set up rsync for that. I feel like I should have registered my WSL for the initial log in to the VM instead of my windows machine. Seems like a missed opportunity.

If anyone has some ideas, suggestions, pointers to where I might find answers to my questions please don’t hold back.

posts.name: Sayan Ghosh
posts.cooked:
rsync should work in WSL.

If you simply want to check if the solutions are correct or not, run the evaluation_file.sh for each assignment. It expects the questions and test cases be present in /opt/se2001/<qs folder> and solutions in ~/se2001/<qs folder> and be run from there.

bash /opt/se2001/$(basename $(pwd))/evaluation_file.sh

You would not need the synchro binary, it is used for maintaining your submissions and for private test cases. Public test cases can be handled simply by the eval files. Feel free to go through the script to understand it better. Here is a very simple dumbed down version: (pseudocode)

for test_case_folder in test_case_folders; do
    diff <(bash/sed/awk students_code < test_case_folder/input.txt) test_case_folder/output.txt
    if [[ $? -eq 0 ]]; then (( passed++ )); fi
    (( total++ ))
done

(( total == passed )) && echo 'All Passed' || echo 'Some failed'

Eval scripts are written by different people and over a span of multiple terms so the exact pattern might be different, but the essence of the script remains the same, take each input.txt from the test cases, feed it to the user’s script, compare its output to the output.txt (expected output).

If you are interested in more details, feel free to reply to this post with your doubts.

posts.name: S.Vignesh
posts.cooked:
Yeah I figured rsync would work in WSL as well but as I said the client machine registered to the VM is my windows system not the WSL. I don’t think I can access the VM from WSL without registering the WSL with passwordless login, right ?

Cool, I will try out running evaluation files. But I just like the synchro commands. The set up is convenient. I can view the problem statement and solve at the same time.

Another doubt I have is now that I have the contents of /opt in my WSL can I just solve the problems directly in the /opt/se2001 folder instead or do the evaluation files stipulate that the solution must be in ~/se2001? I will take a look at the evaluation files to see if I can figure something out.

Thanks for your response.

posts.name: Sayan Ghosh
posts.cooked:
You can create a new key from wsl and upload that key to website, then you can use VM from WSL.

You can create functions in your ~/.bashrc to emulate synchro eval and synchro show.

To make it easy you can simply symlink ~/se2001 to /opt/se2001 instead

posts.name: S.Vignesh
posts.cooked:
Are you sure I can re-register? I remember reading somewhere that the registration of the client machine to the VM is sort of final and if I need to change it I would need to write to support or something.

If I am allowed to register my WSL I am willing to make the shift to my WSL.

Hey, your bash command for evaluation_file.sh works. Thanks, I think I will be able to practice the questions on my local machine as well.

posts.name: Sayan Ghosh
posts.cooked: Yes you can change public key as many times as you want
